idiom_name: AASM state machine on the model + Active Record persistence + callbacks/jobs
implementation_notes: AASM attaches the state machine to the class that persists it: include AASM, declare states, events with guards, and callbacks (before/after, after_commit), and every transition is saved in the model's own column, which makes the process instance a row and gives the happy path for free. Timeouts and compensation remain application code - ActiveJob/Sidekiq for delayed work, explicit compensating events for undo - and the rule that the state change and the outgoing command must not drift is still yours to enforce. Choose AASM when the flow is attached to one model; when the steps belong to other services, a message-based saga is the better fit and AASM only models the local facet.
code_sketch:
class Order < ApplicationRecord
  include AASM

  aasm column: :state do
    state :awaiting_payment, initial: true
    state :awaiting_stock, :done, :compensating

    event :payment_ok do
      transitions from: :awaiting_payment, to: :awaiting_stock,
                  guard: :authorized?, after_commit: :reserve_stock
    end

    event :timeout do                       # fired by a scheduled job
      transitions from: :awaiting_payment, to: :compensating,
                  after_commit: :release_credit
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: after/before callbacks run inside the transition's transaction: a remote call there holds the row lock, so side effects belong in after_commit or in a job.
The bang events (payment_ok!) raise AASM::InvalidTransition while the non-bang form returns false, so a flow that uses both conventions can silently swallow a rejected transition.
A delayed timeout job that reloads a stale object can fire after the state already moved on; re-check the current state inside the job instead of trusting the payload.
AASM persistence writes only the state column; the outgoing command must be enqueued in the same transaction or the classic crash-between-commit-and-send duplication appears.
